On the global regularity of axisymmetric Navier-Stokes-Boussinesq system

Hammadi Abidi Address: Faculté des Sciences de Tunis Email address: Hamadi.Abidi@fst.rnu.tn , Taoufik Hmidi Address: IRMAR, Université de Rennes 1

France Email address: sahbi.keraani@univ-rennes1.fr
Abstract.

In this paper we prove a global well-posedness result for tridimensional Navier-Stokes-Boussinesq system with axisymmetric initial data. This system couples Navier-Stokes equations with a transport equation governing the density.

1. Introduction

The purpose of this paper is to study the global well-posedness for three-dimensional Boussinesq system in the whole space with axisymmetric initial data. This system is described as follows,

(1) {∂tv+v⋅∇v−Δv+∇p=ρez,(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝ3,∂tρ+v⋅∇ρ=0,div​v=0,v|t=0=v0,ρ|t=0=ρ0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v-\Delta v+\nabla p=\rho e_{z},\quad(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{3},\\ \partial_{t}\rho+v\cdot\nabla\rho=0,\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0,\\ v_{|t=0}=v_{0},\quad\rho_{|t=0}=\rho_{0}.\end{array}\right.

Here, the velocity v=(v1,v2,v3)v=(v^{1},v^{2},v^{3}) is a three-component vector field with zero divergence. The scalar function ρ\rho denotes the density which is transported by the flow and acting for the first equation of (1) only in the vertical direction given by eze_{z}. The pressure pp is a scalar function related to the unknowns vv and ρ\rho through an elliptic equation. Remark that when the initial density ρ0\rho_{0} is identically zero then the above system is reduced to the classical Navier-Stokes system which is widely studied:

(2) {∂tv+v⋅∇v−Δ​v+∇p=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v-\Delta v+\nabla p=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v_{0}.\end{array}\right.

Recall that the existence of global weak solutions in the energy space for (2) goes back to J. Leray [23] in the last century. However the uniqueness of these solutions is only known in space dimension two. It is also well-known that smooth solutions are global in dimension two and for higher dimensions when the data are small in some critical spaces; see for instance [21] for more detailed discussions. Although the breakdown of smooth solutions with large initial data is still now an open problem some partial results are known outside the context of small data. We refer for instance to recent papers of J.-Y. Chemin and I. Gallagher [10, 11] where global existence in dimension three is established for special structure of initial data which are not small in any critical space.

There is an interesting case of global existence for (2) corresponding to large initial data but with special geometry, called axisymmetric without swirl. Before going further in the details let us give some general statements about Navier-Stokes system in space dimension three. First, we start with introducing the vorticity which is a physical quantity that plays a significant role in the theory of global existence; for a given vector field vv the vorticity ω\omega is the vector defined by ω=curl​v.\omega={\rm curl}\,v. Thus we get from (2) the vorticity equation

∂tω+v⋅∇ω−Δ​ω=ω⋅∇v.\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega-\Delta\omega=\omega\cdot\nabla v.

According to Beale-Kato-Majda criterion the formation of singularities in finite time is due to the accumulation of the vorticity. In other words, to have global existence it suffices to bound for every time the quantity ‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}. However the main difficulty arising in dimension three is the lack of information about the manner that the vortex-stretching term ω⋅∇v\omega\cdot\nabla\,v affects the dynamic of the fluid.

For the geometry of axisymmetric flows without swirl we have a cancellation in the stretching term giving rise to new conservation laws. We say that a vector field vv is axisymmetric if it has the form:

v⁡(t,x)=vr​(t,r,z)​er+vz​(t,r,z)​ez,x=(x1,x2,z),r=(x12+x22)12,v(t,x)=v^{r}(t,r,z)e_{r}+v^{z}(t,r,z)e_{z},\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2},z),\quad r=({x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}})^{\frac{1}{2}},

where (er,eθ,ez)\big(e_{r},e_{\theta},e_{z}\big) is the cylindrical basis of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and the components vrv^{r} and vzv^{z} do not depend on the angular variable. The main feature of axisymmetric flows arises in the vorticity which takes the form,

ω=(∂zvr−∂rvz)​eθ:=ωθ​eθ\omega=(\partial_{z}v^{r}-\partial_{r}v^{z})e_{\theta}:=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta}

and satisfies

∂tω+v⋅∇ω−Δ​ω=vrr​ω.\partial_{t}\omega+v\cdot\nabla\omega-\Delta\omega=\frac{v^{r}}{r}\omega.

Since the Laplacian operator has the form Δ=∂r​r+1r∂r+∂z​z\Delta=\partial_{rr}+\frac{1}{r}\partial_{r}+\partial_{zz} in the cylindrical coordinates then the component ωθ\omega_{\theta} of the vorticity will satisfy

(3) ∂tωθ+v⋅∇ωθ−Δ​ωθ+ωθr2=vrr​ωθ.\partial_{t}\omega_{\theta}+v\cdot\nabla\omega_{\theta}-\Delta\omega_{\theta}+\frac{\omega_{\theta}}{r^{2}}=\frac{v^{r}}{r}\omega_{\theta}.

Consequently, the quantity Γ:=ωθr\Gamma:=\frac{\omega_{\theta}}{r} obeys to the equation

∂tΓ+v⋅∇Γ−Δ​Γ−2r​∂rΓ=0.\partial_{t}\Gamma+v\cdot\nabla\Gamma-\Delta\Gamma-\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r}\Gamma=0.

Obviously, we have for p≥1,p\geq 1, ∫2r​∂rΓ​|Γ|p−1​(sign ​Γ)​𝑑x≤0{\int\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r}\Gamma|\Gamma|^{p-1}(\textnormal{sign }\Gamma)dx\leq 0} and then we deduce that for all p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty]

‖Γ⁡(t)‖Lp≤‖Γ0‖Lp.\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\Gamma_{0}\|_{L^{p}}.

It was shown by M. Ukhoviskii and V. Yudovich [25] and independently by O. A. Ladyzhenskaya [20] that these conservation laws are strong enough to prevent the formation of singularities in finite time for axisymmetric flows. More precisely, the system (2) has a unique global solution for v0∈H1v_{0}\in H^{1} such that ω0,ω0r∈L2∩L∞.\omega_{0},\frac{\omega_{0}}{r}\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}. Remark that in term of Sobolev regularities these assumptions are satisfied when v0∈Hsv_{0}\in H^{s} with s>72.s>\frac{7}{2}. Few decades afterwards, S. Leonardi, J. Màlek, J. Necăs and M. Pokorný [22] weakened the initial regularity for v0∈H2v_{0}\in H^{2}. This result was recently improved by H. Abidi [1] for v0∈H12v_{0}\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}.

Let us now come back to our first problematic which is the study of global well-posedness for the Boussinesq system (1). In space dimension two many papers are recently devoted to this problem and the study seems to be in a satisfactory state. More precisely we have global existence in different function spaces and for different viscosities, we refer for example to [2, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19].

In the case of space dimension three few results are known about global existence. We recall the result of R. Danchin and M. Paicu [14]. They proved a global well-posedness result for small initial data belonging to some critical Lorentz spaces.

Our goal here is to study the global existence for the system (1) with axisymmetric initial data, which means that the velocity v0v_{0} is assumed to be an axisymmetric vector field without swirl and the density ρ0\rho_{0} depends only on (r,z)(r,z). It should be mentioned that this structure is preserved for strong solutions in their lifespan. Before stating our main result we denote by Πz\Pi_{z} the orthogonal projector over the axis (O​z).(Oz). Our result reads as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let v0∈H1v_{0}\in H^{1} be an axisymmetric vector field with zero divergence and such that ω0r∈L2.\frac{{\omega_{0}}}{r}\in L^{2}. Let ρ0∈L2∩L∞\rho_{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty} depending only on (r,z)(r,z) and such that supp ​ρ0\hbox{supp }\rho_{0} does not intersect the axis (O​z)(Oz) and Πz​(supp ​ρ0)\Pi_{z}(\hbox{supp }\rho_{0}) is a compact set. Then the system (1) has a unique global solution (v,ρ)(v,\rho) such that

v∈C⁡(ℝ+,H1)∩Lloc 1​(ℝ+,W1,∞),v\in{C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{1}_{\textnormal{loc }}(\mathbb{R}_{+};W^{1,\infty}),
ωr∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2),ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2∩L∞).\frac{\omega}{r}\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}),\quad\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}).

The assumption that the density ρ\rho is zero in some region of the space ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} is not very meaningful from a physical point of view. However we can relax this hypothesis and extend our result to more general case: the initial density is assumed to be constant near the axis (O​z)(Oz) and for large value of zz. More precisely, we have the following result.

Corollary 1.2.

Let v0∈H1v_{0}\in H^{1} be an axisymmetric vector field with zero divergence and such that ω0r∈L2.\frac{{\omega_{0}}}{r}\in L^{2}. Let ρ0∈L∞\rho_{0}\in L^{\infty} depending only on (r,z)(r,z) such that ρ0≡c0\rho_{0}\equiv c_{0}, for some constant c0c_{0} in a region of type {x;r≤r0,|z|≥|z0|},\big\{x;r\leq r_{0},|z|\geq|z_{0}|\big\}, with r0>0r_{0}>0 and ρ0−c0∈L2\rho_{0}-c_{0}\in L^{2}. Then the system (1) has a unique global solution (v,ρ)(v,\rho) such that

v∈C⁡(ℝ+,H1)∩Lloc 1​(ℝ+,W1,∞),v\in{C}(\mathbb{R}_{+};H^{1})\cap L^{1}_{\textnormal{loc }}(\mathbb{R}_{+};W^{1,\infty}),
ωr∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2),ρ−c0∈Lloc∞​(ℝ+,L2∩L∞).\frac{\omega}{r}\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}),\quad\rho-c_{0}\in L^{\infty}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{+};L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}).

The proof of this corollary is an immediate consequence of Theorem 1.1. Indeed, we set ρ¯​(t,x)=ρ⁡(t,x)−c0,\bar{\rho}(t,x)=\rho(t,x)-c_{0}, then the system (1) is reduced to

{∂tv+v⋅∇v−Δ​v+∇p−c0​ez=ρ¯​ez∂tρ¯+v⋅∇ρ¯=0div​v=0v|t=0=v0,ρ¯|t=0=ρ0−c0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\partial_{t}v+v\cdot\nabla v-\Delta v+\nabla p-c_{0}e_{z}=\bar{\rho}e_{z}\\ \partial_{t}\bar{\rho}+v\cdot\nabla\bar{\rho}=0\\ \textnormal{div}\,v=0\\ v_{|t=0}=v_{0},\quad\bar{\rho}_{|t=0}=\rho_{0}-c_{0}.\end{array}\right.

Now by changing the pressure pp to p¯=p−c0​z\bar{p}=p-c_{0}z we get the same system (1) and therefore we can apply the results of Theorem 1.1.

Next we shall briefly discuss the new difficulties that one should deal with compared to the system (2). First we start with writing the analogous equation to (3) for the vorticity. An easy computation gives

curl​(ρ​ez)=(∂2ρ∂1ρ0)=−(∂rρ)​eθ.\textnormal{curl}(\rho e_{z})=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{2}\rho\\ \partial_{1}\rho\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=-(\partial_{r}\rho)e_{\theta}.

This yields to

(4) ∂tωθ+v⋅∇ωθ−Δ​ωθ+ωθr2=vrr​ωθ−∂rρ.\partial_{t}\omega_{\theta}+v\cdot\nabla\omega_{\theta}-\Delta\omega_{\theta}+\frac{\omega_{\theta}}{r^{2}}=\frac{v^{r}}{r}\omega_{\theta}-\partial_{r}\rho.

It follows that the evolution of the quantity Γ:=ωθr\Gamma:=\frac{\omega_{\theta}}{r} is governed by the equation

(5) ∂tΓ+v⋅∇Γ−ΔΓ−2r∂rΓ=−∂rρr⋅\partial_{t}\Gamma+v\cdot\nabla\Gamma-\Delta\Gamma-\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r}\Gamma=-\frac{\partial_{r}\rho}{r}\cdot

Since the density ρ\rho satisfies a transport equation then the only conserved quantities that one should use are ‖ρ⁡(t)‖Lp\|\rho(t)\|_{L^{p}} for every p∈[1,∞].p\in[1,\infty]. Loosely speaking, the source term ∂rρr\frac{\partial_{r}\rho}{r} in the equation (5) that one need to estimate has the scale of Δ​ρ\Delta\rho and then to estimate Γ\Gamma in some Lebesgue spaces one can try for example the maximal regularity of the heat semigroup. However it is not at all clear whether we can prove a suitable maximal regularity because the involved elliptic operator −Δ−2r∂r-\Delta-\frac{2}{r}\partial_{r} has singular coefficients . Now, by taking the L2L^{2}-inner product of (5) with Γ\Gamma we are led to estimate the quantity ‖ρ/r‖L2\|\rho/r\|_{L^{2}} which has the scaling of ‖∇ρ‖L2\|\nabla\rho\|_{L^{2}}. In other words we have

‖Γ⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖Γ⁡(τ)‖H˙12​𝑑τ≤‖Γ0‖L22+∫0t‖(ρ/r)​(τ)‖L22​𝑑τ.\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\Gamma(\tau)\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}^{2}d\tau\leq\|\Gamma_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|(\rho/r)(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau.

Remark that the quantity ‖ρ/r‖L2\|\rho/r\|_{L^{2}} is not well-defined if we don’t assume at least that ρ⁡(t,0,z)=0.\rho(t,0,z)=0. As we have seen previously in the statement of Theorem 1.1 we need more than this latter condition: the initial density ρ0\rho_{0} has to be supported far from the axis (O​z).(Oz). To follow the evolution of the quantity ‖ρ⁡(t)/r‖L2\|\rho(t)/r\|_{L^{2}} the approach that consists in writing the equation of ρ⁡(t)r\frac{\rho(t)}{r} fails because it gives an exponential growth,

‖ρ⁡(t)/r‖L2≤‖ρ0/r‖L2​e‖vr/r‖Lt1​L∞.\|\rho(t)/r\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\rho_{0}/r\|_{L^{2}}e^{\|v^{r}/r\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}}.

Our idea to perform this growth relies in studying some dynamic aspects of the support of ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) which is nothing but the transported of the initial support by the flow. We need particularly to get a proper low bound about the distance from the axis (O​z)(Oz) of the support of ρ⁡(t),\rho(t), see Proposition 3.2. To reach this target and once again the axisymmetry property of the flow will play a crucial role since the trajectories of the particles are contained in the meridional plane. This approach allows us to improve the exponential growth for ‖ρ⁡(t)/r‖L2\|\rho(t)/r\|_{L^{2}} to a quadratic estimate. Roughly speaking we obtain the estimate

‖ρ⁡(t)/r‖L2≤C0​‖vr/r‖Lt1​L∞​(1+‖v‖Lt1​L∞).\|\rho(t)/r\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{0}\|v^{r}/r\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\big(1+\|v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\big).

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section 22 we recall some basic ingredients of Littlwood-Paley theory. In section 33 we study some qualitative and analytic properties of the flow associated to an axisymmetric vector field. In section 44 we give some global a priori estimates. The proof of Theorem 1.1 is done in Section 5.5.

3. Study of the flow map

The main goal of this section is to study some geometric and analytic properties of the generalized flow map associated to an axisymmetric vector field.

ψ⁡(t,s,x)=x+∫stv⁡(τ,ψ⁡(τ,s,x))​𝑑τ.\psi(t,s,x)=x+\int_{s}^{t}v(\tau,\psi(\tau,s,x))d\tau.

This part will be the cornerstone of the proof of Theorem 1.1. We need first to recall some basic results about the generalized flow. If the vector field vv belongs to Lloc1​(ℝ,Cb1)L^{1}_{\textnormal{loc}}(\mathbb{R},C^{1}_{b}) then the generalized flow is uniquely determined and exists globally in time. Here Cb1C^{1}_{b} denotes the space of functions with continuous bounded gradient. In addition, for every t,s∈ℝt,s\in\mathbb{R}, ψ⁡(t,s)\psi(t,s) is a diffeomorphism that preserves Lebesgue measure when div ​v=0\textnormal{div }v=0 and

ψ−1​(t,s,x)=ψ⁡(s,t,x).\psi^{-1}(t,s,x)=\psi(s,t,x).

Now we define the distance from a given point xx to a subset A⊂ℝ3A\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} by

d⁡(x,A):=infy∈A‖x−y‖,d(x,A):=\inf_{y\in A}\|x-y\|,

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is the usual Euclidian norm. The distance between two subsets AA and BB of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} is defined by

d⁡(A,B):=infx∈A,y∈B‖x−y‖.d(A,B):=\inf_{x\in A,y\in B}\|x-y\|.

The diameter of a bounded subset A⊂ℝ3A\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} is defined by

diam ​A=supx,y∈A‖x−y‖.\textnormal{diam }A=\sup_{x,y\in A}\|x-y\|.

Our first result is the following.

Proposition 3.1.

Let vv be a smooth axisymmetric vector field and ψ⁡(t,s)\psi(t,s) its flow. Let x∉(O​z)x\notin(Oz) and r⁡(x):=d⁡(x,(O​z))r(x):=d(x,(Oz)), then

  1. (1)

    For every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, the trajectory Γx,s:={ψ⁡(t,s,x),t∈ℝ}\Gamma_{x,s}:=\big\{\psi(t,s,x),t\in\mathbb{R}\big\} is a smooth curve contained in the meridional plan.

  2. (2)

    For every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, the trajectory Γx,s\Gamma_{x,s} does not intersect the axis (O​z)(Oz), that is Γx,s∩(O​z)=∅.\Gamma_{x,s}\cap(Oz)=\varnothing. More precisely,

    r⁡(x)​e−|∫st‖vrr​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ|≤d⁡(ψ⁡(t,s,x),(O​z))≤r⁡(x)​e|∫st‖vrr​(τ)‖L∞​𝑑τ|.r(x)\displaystyle{e^{-|\int_{s}^{t}\|\frac{v^{r}}{r}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau|}}\leq d(\psi(t,s,x),(Oz))\leq r(x)e^{|\int_{s}^{t}\|\frac{v^{r}}{r}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}d\tau|}.
Proof.

(1) We start with the decomposition of the vector xx in the cylindrical basis:

x=r⁡(x)​(cos⁡θxsin⁡θx0)+zx​ez,withrx>0.x=r(x)\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta_{x}\\ \sin\theta_{x}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}+z_{x}e_{z},\quad\hbox{with}\quad r_{x}>0.

We decompose also the generalized flow ψ⁡(t,s,x)\psi(t,s,x) in the cylindrical coordinates

ψ⁡(t,s,x)=r⁡(t,s,x)​(cos⁡(θ⁡(t,s,x))sin⁡(θ⁡(t,s,x))0)+z⁡(t,s,x)​ez.\psi(t,s,x)=r(t,s,x)\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta(t,s,x))\\ \sin(\theta(t,s,x))\\ 0\end{pmatrix}+z(t,s,x)e_{z}.

Since vv is smooth in space-time variables then the flow map ψ⁡(t,s,x)\psi(t,s,x) is also smooth. Now we intend to prove that r⁡(t,s,x)r(t,s,x) remains strictly positive for all t,s∈ℝt,s\in\mathbb{R}. Assume that there exist t1,s1∈ℝt_{1},s_{1}\in\mathbb{R} such that ψ⁡(t1,s1,x)\psi(t_{1},s_{1},x) belongs to the axis (O​z).(Oz). 4. A priori estimates

This section is devoted to the a priori estimates needed for the proof of Theorem 1.1. We distinguish especially two kinds: the first one deals with some easy estimates that one can obtained by energy estimates. However the second one is concerned with some strong estimates which are the heart of the proof of our main result.

4.1. Weak a priori estimates

We will prove the following energy estimates.

Proposition 4.1.

Let v0∈L2v_{0}\in L^{2} be a vector field with zero divergence and ρ0∈L2∩L∞.\rho_{0}\in L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}. Then every smooth solution of (1) satisfies

‖ρ⁡(t)‖L2∩L∞≤‖ρ0‖L2∩L∞.\|\rho(t)\|_{L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}}\leq\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}\cap L^{\infty}}.
‖v⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L22​𝑑τ≤C0​(1+t2).\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau\leq C_{0}(1+t^{2}).
Proof.

The first estimate is obvious since the flow preserves Lebesgue measure. For the second one we take the L2L^{2}-inner product of the velocity equation with vv. Then we get after some integration by parts

(8) 12​dd​t​‖v⁡(t)‖L22+‖∇v​(t)‖L22≤‖v⁡(t)‖L2​‖ρ⁡(t)‖L2.\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\nabla v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\|\rho(t)\|_{L^{2}}.

After simplification that one can rigorously justify, the last inequality leads to

dd​t​‖v⁡(t)‖L2≤‖ρ⁡(t)‖L2.\frac{d}{dt}\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|\rho(t)\|_{L^{2}}.

Integrating in time this inequality yields

‖v⁡(t)‖L2≤‖v0‖L2+∫0t‖ρ⁡(τ)‖L2​𝑑τ.\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\rho(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}d\tau.

Since ‖ρ⁡(t)‖L2=‖ρ0‖L2,\|\rho(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}}, then

‖v⁡(t)‖L2≤‖v0‖L2+t​‖ρ0‖L2.\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}}+t\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

Putting this estimate into (8) gives

12​‖v⁡(t)‖L22+∫0t‖∇v​(τ)‖L22​𝑑τ≤12​‖v0‖L22+(‖v0‖L2+t​‖ρ0‖L2)​‖ρ0‖L2​t.\frac{1}{2}\|v(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{t}\|\nabla v(\tau)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}d\tau\leq\frac{1}{2}\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\big(\|v_{0}\|_{L^{2}}+t\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}}\big)\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}}t.

This gives the desired estimate and the demonstration of the proposition is now accomplished. ∎

The next proposition describes some estimates linking the velocity to the vorticity by the use of the so-called Bio-Savart law.

Proposition 4.2.

Let vv be a smooth axisymmetric vector field with zero divergence and denote ω=ωθ​eθ\omega=\omega_{\theta}e_{\theta} its curl. Then

  1. (1)
    ‖v‖L∞≤C​‖ωθ‖L212​‖ωθ‖H˙112.\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}^{\frac{1}{2}}.

    ‖vr/r‖L∞≤C​‖ωθ/r‖L212​‖ωθ/r‖H˙112.\|v^{r}/r\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\|\omega_{\theta}/r\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\omega_{\theta}/r\|_{\dot{H}^{1}}^{\frac{1}{2}}.

v⁡(x)=14​π​∫ℝ3(y−x)∧ω⁡(y)|y−x|3​𝑑y.v(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{(y-x)\wedge\omega(y)}{|y-x|^{3}}dy.

:⁣=\displaystyle:= J1​(x)+J2​(x).\displaystyle J_{1}(x)+J_{2}(x).

≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖ωθ‖L6​λ12.\displaystyle\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{6}}\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}.

For the second integral we use again Hölder inequalities

‖J2‖L∞\displaystyle\|J_{2}\|_{L^{\infty}} ≤\displaystyle\leq ‖ωθ‖L2​(∫|x|≥λ1|x|4​𝑑x)12\displaystyle\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{2}}\Big(\int_{|x|\geq\lambda}\frac{1}{|x|^{4}}dx\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}

This yields

∥v∥L∞≲|ωθ∥L6λ12+∥ωθ∥L2λ−12.\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\ |\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{6}}\lambda^{\frac{1}{2}}+\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{2}}\lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

By choosing λ=‖ωθ‖L2‖ωθ‖L6\lambda=\frac{\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{2}}}{\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{6}}} we get

‖v‖L∞≲‖ωθ‖L212​‖ωθ‖L612.\|v\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\omega_{\theta}\|_{L^{6}}^{\frac{1}{2}}.

|vr/r|​(x)≲(1|⋅|2⋆|ωθ/r|)​(x).|v^{r}/r|(x)\lesssim\big(\frac{1}{|\cdot|^{2}}\star|\omega_{\theta}/r|\big)(x).

Now we conclude similarly to the first estimate. ∎

The last estimate of Proposition (9) is a direct consequence of the embedding Bp,13p+1↪W1,∞B_{p,1}^{\frac{3}{p}+1}\hookrightarrow W^{1,\infty} and the proof is then accomplished. ∎

5. Proof of the main result

The existence part can be done in a classical way for example by smoothing out the initial data. However we have to use an appropriate approximation that does not alter never the initial geometric structure nor the uniform estimates in the space of initial data. We will work with the approximation of the identity and show that it has the requested properties: let ϕ\phi be a smooth positive radial function with support contained in B⁡(0,1)B(0,1) and such that ϕ≡1\phi\equiv 1 in a neighborhood of zero. We assume that ∫ℝ3ϕ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1.\displaystyle{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\phi(x)dx=1.} For every n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*} we set ϕn​(x)=n3​ϕ​(n​x)\phi_{n}(x)={n^{3}}\phi(nx) and we define the family

v0,n=ϕn⋆v0andρ0,n=ϕn⋆ρ0.v_{0,n}=\phi_{n}\star v_{0}\quad\textnormal{and}\quad\rho_{0,n}=\phi_{n}\star\rho_{0}.

We will start with the following stability results.

    ∫ℝ3(ρn)2​(t,x)r2​𝑑x≤1r02​‖ρ0‖L22+2​‖ρ0‖L∞​(ln⁡2+‖vr/r‖Lt1​L∞)​(d0+‖v‖Lt1​L∞).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{{{(\rho^{n})}^{2}(t,x)}}{r^{2}}dx\leq\frac{1}{r_{0}^{2}}\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+2\|\rho_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}}\big(\ln 2+\|{v^{r}}/{r}\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\big)\big(d_{0}+\|v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}\big).

The estimate of the part (2) of the above lemma is little bit different from part (2) of Corollary 3.3 because we have an additional linear term ‖v‖Lt1​L∞\|v\|_{L^{1}_{t}L^{\infty}}. Nevertheless, the presence of this term does not deeply affect the calculus seen before in the a priori estimates; we obtain at the end the same estimates of Proposition 4.3.

Proof.

(1) The fact that the vector field v0,nv_{0,n} is axisymmetric is due to the radial property of the functions ϕn\phi_{n}, for more details see [3]. The estimate of v0,nv_{0,n} in H1H^{1} is easy to obtain by using the classical properties of the convolution operation combined with ‖ϕn‖L1=1.\|\phi_{n}\|_{L^{1}}=1. Let us now come back to the proof of the existence part of Theorem 1.1. We have just seen in Lemma 5.1 that the initial structure of axisymmetry is preserved for every nn and the involved norms are uniformly controlled with respect to this parameter nn. Thus we can construct locally in time a unique solution (vn,θn)(v_{n},\theta_{n}) that does not blow up in finite time since the Lipschitz norm of the velocity is well controlled as it was stated in Proposition 4.3. By standard arguments we can show that this family converges to (v,θ)(v,\theta) which satisfies in turn our IVP. We omit here the details which are very classical and we will next focus on the uniqueness part. Set
